pages.text:
*Way to Lose #19: Keep score of a game that has no score.*

Coach Gin walks to the sideline where the little plastic scoreboard hangs from a wire, displaying a zero to zero score that feels heavier than the actual numbers. She looks at it, then at the team, and whistles. The sound is short and sharp, like the zipper on a heavy winter coat.

"New rule," she says, her voice calm as a lake in summer. "We are not playing a game. We are playing a scrimmage."

She takes the scoreboard down. It swings on its cord, clicking against the chain-link fence with a sound like loose change. She puts it in the back pocket of her windbreaker. The plastic digits are still there, glowing faintly in the sun, but no one is looking.

"Rule one," Gin says. "If you keep score, you sit out."

Josie gasps. "But how do we know if we won?"

"We don't care," Gin says. "Rule two. Every single one of you has to touch the ball before anyone shoots."

Ahmed crosses his arms. "That's inefficient."

"Efficiency is for machines," Gin says. "You are human. Touch it."

She points to the field. The grass is muddy and slants to the left, just like always. I look at the empty spot on the fence where the scoreboard used to be. My brain tries to fill the gap with numbers, but it fails.

The ball is in the air.
pages.image: Coach Gin in a yellow windbreaker removing a small plastic scoreboard with only small round lights from a chain-link fence at a muddy soccer field; a wiry girl with a yellow armband watches closely; the field slants slightly to one side with a duck pond in the background.

pages.text:
The first ten minutes are a disaster. Mostly because I am running, breathing hard, and counting touches, but I cannot count the score, which is the part I actually care about.

I keep checking the sidelines to see if Dad is writing it down on his foam finger. He is not. He is just cheering, which is unhelpful. Josie is on the wing, vibrating with energy because she cannot say the score. So she has invented a new language. She whistles a high, thin note when things are good. A low, grumpy squeak when they are bad. Right now, she is producing a complex, buzzing chord that sounds exactly like a mouse trapped in a shoebox.

I have the ball at midfield. I look left, then right, trying to remember who is supposed to be open. My brain is glitching. It is flickering with ghostly, angry numbers that refuse to load.

"Touched!" Tank shouts. He has just bumped the ball gently into the mud.

I feel a spike of irritation in my chest. Why does this feel so wrong? I am missing the thing that tells me if I am doing a good job. Without the number, I am just a girl kicking a ball. That is a terrifying concept.

I pass to Priya. She is standing in the box with her eyes squeezed shut. I hope she likes the ball. And, more importantly, I hope she doesn't start counting.
pages.image: A talkative girl with wild curly hair whistling loudly while a large gentle boy in a red jersey gently touches a soccer ball; the muddy field is empty of spectators; the mood is tense and slightly absurd.

pages.text:
Something changes around minute twelve. I am watching Tank, who is usually so polite he apologizes to the grass if he steps on it. He faces off against the opposing striker, but he does not say "Excuse me" or "Pardon my intrusion." He simply steps in, plants his feet, and uses his shoulder to win the ball without a single word of regret.

I blink, wondering if I have accidentally entered a dream where Tank has become a shark. He looks around, and for the first time in my entire soccer career, he does not look like he is waiting for someone to say it is okay to exist.

Then Priya does something even weirder. A cross comes in, high and hard, the kind that usually makes her flinch like she has been touched by a wasp. She does not close her eyes. She stands in the box, gloves up, eyes wide open. The ball bounces off her glove and out of play. She did not whisper. She did not shrink. She just stood there, looking at the ball like it had personally offended her.

The twins, Leo and Mateo, are running together. They are not arguing. They are looking at each other. Leo points. Mateo nods. They pass the ball to each other, clean and fast, without checking their birth certificates to see who is older.

The air in the park feels different. It is lighter. The mud is still mud, but it feels less heavy.

I am still counting. But the numbers are quieter.
pages.image: A large gentle boy in a red jersey successfully challenging an opponent for the ball; a tiny girl with glasses and oversized gloves stands alert in the goal; two identical boys pass a ball to each other without arguing.

pages.text:
I have the ball at midfield, and Ahmed is already closing in. He is fast, a human blur that never seems to have brakes, and usually he simply takes the ball and runs. Today, though, he takes it and stops abruptly.

The opposing defender is right there, a wall of jersey blocking the only way forward. Ahmed looks trapped, his eyes wide with the specific panic of a kid who has forgotten his homework. He looks at me, and I yell, "Move!"

He glances back at the defender, then back at me, before kicking the ball to me in a messy, desperate arc that is not great. I catch it. I am in the box, the goal is right there, and the net is empty. I kick it.

It goes in.

Silence falls over the park. Ahmed stands still, staring at the ball in the net, then looks at me with his mouth hanging open. "Was that..." he starts.

"Passing," I say.

"Yeah," he says, scratching his head. "It was faster than I thought."

I start to laugh, a sound I cannot stop, and I have to sit down on the wet grass to keep from falling over. My armband slips off my shoulder, but I do not care.
pages.image: A wiry girl with a yellow armband sitting on wet grass laughing hysterically; a lanky fast boy stands nearby looking confused and surprised; a soccer ball rests in the net behind them.

pages.text:
The scrimmage ends when Gin blows her whistle, a sharp crack that cuts through the humid air. She walks over to us, thermos in hand, and takes a long sip. The tea smells like dirt and determination.

"Who won?" she asks.

We look at each other. Josie shrugs, then Tank shrugs, and even Ahmed looks confused, which is a new experience for him.

"I don't know," I say, because the truth is I really have no idea.

"Good," Gin says. "That is the point."

I walk back to the bus, my legs feeling like they are made of wet clay. My heart is beating in my chest, but it is not pounding with fear or panic. It is just beating, steady and strong, like a drum in a quiet room. I feel tired in a good way, the kind of tired that comes from running until you forget to worry about the score. It feels like finishing a math test and realizing you actually liked the numbers.

I pull out my red notebook, the Loss Log, and flip to the back where the Strategy Log lives. I pick up my pen, my hand hovering over the page.

I write: *Tired. Good.*

I look at the line. It is small, but it is true. I close the notebook and shove it deep into my backpack, underneath the bag of orange slices. I am a little embarrassed, but I keep it there, safe and solid, like a secret I am ready to share.
pages.image: A wiry girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband hiding a red notebook in a backpack; a small coach with a silver braid stands nearby holding a steel thermos; the mood is quiet and reflective.
